summary.text: Your company phone and website differ across the public pages buyers check, so a customer can reach a line your own site never prints.
The domain behind your published email expires on 2026-12-04 and has no transfer lock, so quotes and tender mail can stop arriving.
Your rating of 4.7 from 32 reviews is a real asset, and none of your newest reviews carries an owner reply.

titles.f1: The domain behind your published email is unlocked and can lapse, taking quotes with it.
titles.f2: Anyone can forge email from the address on your site, so a client can be fooled by an invoice.
titles.f3: The domain you call canonical can be used to forge supplier or director emails.
titles.f4: A Google check flags your robots file as invalid, so directories can outrank your own site.
titles.f5: The phone field on your LinkedIn page is broken, so a recruiter or buyer cannot call you.
titles.f6: None of your newest Google reviews has an owner reply, so a bad rating sits unanswered.
titles.f7: Your enquiry site is missing its security headers, so browsers and scanners flag it to visitors.
titles.f8: AI assistants cannot tell who wrote your site or when, so they quote competitors instead.
titles.f9: A contractor profile under your registration number shows a placeholder phone and no projects.
titles.c1: Your head office unit number differs across three public pages, so a courier can reach the wrong door.
titles.c2: Your head office phone differs between sources, so a customer may call a line your site never prints.
titles.c3: Your contact email differs between your two site families, so prospects write to two mailboxes.
titles.c4: Three websites are presented as yours, so search engines and buyers split your enquiries.
titles.c5: An employer profile names a different legal entity, so a candidate or a bank sees another company.
titles.c6: Your headcount differs across three public pages, which invites questions in tender and credit checks.
titles.c7: Your branch list differs between your site and directories, so a customer cannot find the nearest office.
titles.c8: Your contractor grade differs between your site and a directory, so a tender panel sees a weaker record.
titles.c9: Your completed project count differs across three pages, which weakens the biggest number you own.
titles.n1: A poor rating under a name that matches one of your own engineers is worth checking.
titles.n2: Some of your top reviews share one date, which a careful buyer may read as arranged.
titles.n3: Your branch number sits one digit from your head office line — worth checking it is not a typo.
titles.n4: A directory lists you as small installations only, which may undercut your commercial work.
titles.n5: Your calculator's accuracy claim sits against your own site's caveat — worth checking the wording.
titles.n6: One site promises a fast installation window and the other a longer one — worth checking which applies.
titles.n7: Your mobile site scores well below desktop, which may cost you enquiries from phones.
titles.n8: A turnover figure is in circulation from an earlier year, worth checking before a bank sees it.
titles.n9: A glowing review carries a name that matches someone on your team — worth checking.
titles.n10: Lifetime energy generated is published as two different totals, worth checking which is current.
titles.n11: Two tools disagree on whether your robots file is valid, so worth checking which one is right.
